Cross-Validate Estimated Scales with Explicit Folds

Source: R/cross_validate.R
cross_validate.Rd

Estimate the scales of effect and the GLM coefficients again inside every fold, using only that fold's training rows, then score the predictions for the rows it holds out. A fold is one split of the data into analysis rows, which fit the model, and assessment rows, which are held out and predicted. Use this function to ask how well a scale-of-effect model predicts observations it never saw.

Usage

cross_validate(
  formula,
  data,
  kernel_inputs,
  folds,
  family = c("gaussian", "poisson", "binomial", "nbinom2", "Gamma"),
  backend = c("profile_glm", "refit", "joint_nb2"),
  weights = NULL,
  optim_args = list(),
  glm_control = stats::glm.control(),
  metrics = NULL,
  keep_fits = FALSE,
  keep_selection = FALSE,
  theta = NULL,
  dispersion = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_cv'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

formula

Two-sided model formula, written as for stats::glm(). The response must be a column of data, optionally wrapped in I(), or cbind(successes, failures) for grouped binomial data. Create any other transformed response as a column before the call. Predictors can include factors, interactions, offsets, and the data-dependent terms described in "Formula terms that learn from the data". Every variable must be a column of data or a covariate prepared in kernel_inputs, and at least one predictor must be a covariate whose scale is optimized.

data

Data frame with one row per observation, holding the raw responses and every nonspatial predictor. Its row names are the row IDs. They must be unique and must be the same set of IDs as the row names of kernel_inputs$kernel_dat. The folds refer to rows by these IDs. Spatial covariate columns are rebuilt inside every fold, so any values data holds for them are ignored. Rows with missing values are never dropped silently, so a fold that contains one fails.

kernel_inputs

A multiScaleR_data object from kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group() for the same observations. It must keep the cell-level distances and values (store_cell_data = TRUE, the default), because every fold rebuilds its covariates from the raw cells. Lean objects are rejected. Choose max_D, the starting scales, and any metric definitions without looking at the assessment outcomes.

folds

Named list of explicit splits, for example from grouped_cv_folds() or spatial_cv_folds(). Each split is a list of two character vectors of row IDs, analysis and assessment, which must not overlap. A row can be left out of a split entirely (for example, by a spatial buffer) and can be assessed in more than one split. Keep rows that share a site, animal, or other sampling unit on the same side of every split.

family

Character response family. Choose "gaussian" (identity link, the default), "poisson" (log), "binomial" (logit), "nbinom2" (negative binomial, log), or "Gamma" (log). Lowercase "gamma" is accepted. For "nbinom2" the variance is mu + mu^2 / theta, where mu is the expected count and theta the size parameter, so a small theta means strong extra variation. For "Gamma" the variance is dispersion x mu^2. Other links and quasi-likelihood families are not supported.

backend

Fitting route for the scales, passed to multiScale_optim(). The default "profile_glm" is the fast analytic route. "refit" refits the GLM at every trial scale and accepts formula terms the default rejects, such as a spline of an optimized covariate without fixed knots. "joint_nb2" estimates the scales, coefficients, and theta together, and applies only to family = "nbinom2" with theta estimated. If you leave backend unset, "Gamma" and an NB2 model with a fixed theta use "refit", the only route they support. Naming another backend for them is an error. The usual starting-value, convergence, and kernel or metric checks of multiScale_optim() apply in every fold. See multiScaleR-fitting-methods.

weights

Optional case frequencies, one nonnegative whole number per row of data in the same order. If the vector has names, they must equal the row names. A weight of 3 counts the row three times. A weight of 0 keeps the row in the records but out of the fit and the scores. The default NULL gives every row a weight of one. Gaussian models accept only weights of one. For binomial data, put the trial counts in a cbind(successes, failures) response, not in weights. Weighted proportions are rejected. Some scale-fitting backends add their own weight requirements.

optim_args

Named list of extra multiScale_optim() arguments used in every fold, such as par or profile_control. Supply radius_grid with backend = "refit" to profile hard radii, together with any smooth scales, in each training split. Supply covariate_transform = "raw" with backend = "refit" to keep optimized covariates in their own units (see "Keep optimized covariates in their own units"). Arguments that supply data, the starting model, a custom refit function, parallel workers, backend, or verbose are reserved. Every fold runs on one worker. The default list() keeps the backend's own defaults. Choose starting values without using the assessment outcomes.

glm_control

Named list of stats::glm.control() settings for the initial GLM fitted to the analysis rows of each fold. The default keeps the settings of glm().

metrics

Optional character vector of scores to record. The defaults depend on family. They are c("rmse", "mae") for Gaussian, c("rmse", "mae", "neg_log_score", "deviance") for Poisson, c("neg_log_score", "brier") for binomial, and c("rmse", "mae", "neg_log_score") for NB2 and Gamma. You can request a subset of the defaults, but not other scores. NB2 and Gamma leave out the deviance because its value depends on theta or the dispersion, which makes it unsuitable for comparing models. Lower is better for every score, and the multiScaleR_cv page defines each one.

keep_fits

Logical. The default FALSE keeps the predictions, scores, fold estimates, and compact diagnostics. TRUE also keeps the full fitted model of every fold in fits, which can use much more memory. You need full fits only to inspect the fold models or to have select_cv() return the selected fits.

keep_selection

Logical. TRUE keeps a compact record of each fold's training likelihood and parameter count in selection_records, which is what select_cv() needs when keep_fits = FALSE. The records come from the fits already run, so they add no fitting time. The default is FALSE.

theta

Optional NB2 size parameter fixed in advance, one positive number. The default NULL estimates theta separately from the analysis rows of each fold. A fixed theta adds no parameter to K (the parameter count used by AIC) and requires the "refit" backend. Fix it only from information independent of the assessment outcomes. Other families reject it.

dispersion

Optional Gamma dispersion fixed in advance, one positive number. The default NULL estimates it in each fold as the training deviance divided by the sum of the frequency weights, the value native Gamma AIC uses. A fixed dispersion adds no parameter to K and is built into the Gamma density before fitting. Fix it only from information independent of the assessment outcomes. Other families reject it.

x

A multiScaleR_cv result, for print().

...

Not used. Reserved for future print controls.

Value

cross_validate() returns a list of class multiScaleR_cv, with class multiScaleR_distribution_cv added for "nbinom2" and "Gamma". Read complete first, then summary (pooled scores), metrics (scores per fold), predictions (one row per held-out observation), fold_results, and training (the scales and coefficients estimated in each fold). See multiScaleR_cv for every element and how to read each score. print() shows how many folds were scored and the pooled scores, and returns x invisibly.

How each fold is fitted

Suppose you estimated sigma, the kernel scale, once from all of the data and then cross-validated only the regression. Every held-out row would already have helped choose the scale that defines its own predictors, and the scores would flatter the model. cross_validate() avoids this by repeating the whole fit inside each fold, using the analysis rows alone.

  1. Rebuild each spatial covariate from the raw cells at the starting scales in kernel_inputs, then center and scale it with the analysis-row mean and standard deviation. Each covariate must have a positive, finite standard deviation in the analysis rows.

  2. Fit the initial GLM to the analysis rows.

  3. Estimate the scales and coefficients with multiScale_optim(). No fit to the full data is used as a starting point.

  4. Rebuild the assessment covariates with the fitted scales, the training standardization, and the training distance bins, then predict the expected response and score it.

The fold fails if the initial GLM, the final GLM, or the scale optimizer does not converge. Folds run one after another, and a failed fold is recorded and never retried.

Build the folds

Row names tie the pieces together. Before any fitting, the function checks that every split names known, unique IDs and that its analysis and assessment rows do not overlap. It cannot check ecological independence from the IDs you supply. Keep observations that share a site, animal, year, or other sampling unit on the same side of each split, and choose the design before you look at any scores.

Rows left out of a split, such as those removed by a buffer, are neither fitted nor scored in that split. A row assessed in several splits is scored each time, every occurrence enters the pooled scores, and assessment_counts records how often each row was assessed. A factor level present in the assessment rows but absent from the analysis rows makes that fold fail at prediction. No zero effect is substituted. vignette("v08-cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR") compares random, grouped, spatial, and buffered fold designs on the same model.

Choose a family and scores

familyLinkDefault metricsBackend when unset
"gaussian"identityrmse, mae"profile_glm"
"poisson"logrmse, mae, neg_log_score, deviance"profile_glm"
"binomial"logitneg_log_score, brier"profile_glm"
"nbinom2"logrmse, mae, neg_log_score"profile_glm", or "refit" with a fixed theta
"Gamma"logrmse, mae, neg_log_score"refit"

Lower is better for every score. RMSE and MAE judge only the predicted mean, in the units of the response. The negative log score judges the whole predicted distribution, so it also penalizes a model that is too confident. Binomial responses can be 0/1 numbers, logical values, a two-level factor, or cbind(successes, failures). cross_validate_glm() explains how binomial log and Brier scores are weighted, and the multiScaleR_cv page defines every score.

Negative binomial and Gamma responses

Both families carry a nuisance parameter, a parameter of the response distribution that is not part of the mean model. It is theta for NB2 and the dispersion for Gamma. Unless you fix it with theta or dispersion, each fold estimates it from the analysis rows and freezes it to score the assessment rows. The negative log score therefore uses a complete, normalized density that the held-out outcomes did not help shape. The frozen value of each fold is stored in distribution and repeated in the theta and dispersion columns of predictions.

  • An estimated nuisance parameter adds one to the native K, and a fixed one adds zero. The native nobs counts rows with positive weight, not the sum of the weights.

  • Estimated Gamma dispersion is the training deviance divided by the sum of the frequency weights, the value native Gamma AIC uses. It differs from the Pearson dispersion that summary() uses for coefficient standard errors, and it does not replace that standard-error convention. A fixed Gamma dispersion is built into the Gamma density before fitting, so the likelihood, AIC, and K agree. Setting only the dispersion field of a native Gamma family would leave its AIC estimating the dispersion from the deviance.

  • NB2 responses must be nonnegative whole numbers and Gamma responses strictly positive, including rows with zero weight.

  • A theta warning from the native NB2 fit, such as a reached iteration limit, makes the fold fail. The warning is kept in warnings.

  • backend = "joint_nb2" starts the coefficients from a GLM with theta = 1 and then estimates theta jointly with the scales. That starting value is neither a fixed theta nor a prior. A fold reports an infinite theta, the exact Poisson limit, only when the joint fit verifies and flags that limit. A large finite theta never stands in for it.

A Gamma model for a strictly positive response uses the same call, and the backend switches to "refit" on its own, for example cross_validate(mass ~ habitat, dat, inputs, folds, family = "Gamma"). Compare NB2 and Poisson candidates with the negative log score on the same counts. cv_tab() lists the comparisons each family allows.

Formula terms that learn from the data

Some formula terms learn constants from the data. scale() learns a mean and standard deviation, poly() learns polynomial coefficients, and splines::ns() and splines::bs() learn knots. In each fold these constants come from the analysis rows and are reused unchanged for the assessment rows. This holds with or without a base::, stats::, or splines:: prefix, and inside arithmetic, I(), pointwise functions such as log(), and offsets. For spatial covariates the constants come from the final fitted training values, not the starting-scale values. Arguments you fix in the formula, such as knots, stay fixed. Coefficients, standard errors, likelihoods, and K are those of the native fit, and fits kept with keep_fits = TRUE carry the same training constants.

Only these four functions are recognized, and only with numeric inputs and supported arguments. An unsupported argument makes the fold fail. Any other operation that learns from the data, such as mean(x) inside a formula or your own transformation function, is not detected. Compute it within each analysis split and apply it unchanged to the assessment rows, or the scores will leak assessment information. For the same reason, do not supply predictors standardized with all rows. Every variable must still be a column of data or a prepared covariate. Variables are never taken from the formula's environment.

With the default "profile_glm" backend, a spline of an optimized covariate needs fixed knots and Boundary.knots and no df. Otherwise the fold fails with a message that names the fix. backend = "refit" accepts adaptive splines.

Keep optimized covariates in their own units

By default each fold centers and scales every optimized covariate with its analysis-row mean and standard deviation, so a coefficient is the effect of a one standard deviation change. With backend = "refit", the setting optim_args = list(covariate_transform = "raw") skips that final step for the optimized covariates. They keep the units of their kernel or metric calculation, such as a kernel-weighted proportion of habitat. Use this when a fixed spline knot or another formula constant is meant in those units.

The initial fit and every scale refit within a fold use the same units, and prediction applies a center of zero and a scale of one. Covariates whose scales are not optimized are still standardized with analysis-row values, and normalization applied upstream, such as the reference normalization of surface metrics, is unchanged. Assessment rows never choose the transformation, the knots, or the scale. Decide on raw units, and on any knots in those units, before you look at the results. Because a change of units can alter a constrained or nonlinear model, compare the two versions by their held-out scores rather than assume they are equivalent.

Use separate maps for groups of surveys

Inputs from kernel_prep_by_group(), which take each row's covariates from its own map (for example, the map of its survey year), are supported. Before fitting, the function checks that the named raster_group labels align with the prepared row IDs. It records the map labels of each fold's analysis and assessment rows in raster_groups. Standardization and distance bins still come from the pooled analysis rows. The map labels are fixed inputs. They add no random effects, no extra parameters, and no scales that vary among maps. Group effects you write in the formula, such as a year factor, keep their native fit, parameter count, and new-level check. See vignette("v06-year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR").

Distance bins and the extraction envelope

When kernel_inputs holds distance-binned summaries (kernel_prep() with bin = TRUE, the default), each fold rebuilds them. The bin edges span max_D plus half a cell diagonal, so cells that intersect the buffer but whose centers lie just beyond max_D keep their values. These edges depend on the declared geometry only, not on any data. The representative distance of each bin is the mean cell distance in that bin over the analysis rows, and the assessment rows reuse it. Inputs saved by older versions of kernel_prep() lack the cell geometry and keep the stricter rule that every cell center lies within max_D. If such inputs are rejected, prepare them again with the current kernel_prep().

Check every fold before comparing models

Read complete first. TRUE means every planned fold was fitted and scored. When a fold fails, complete is FALSE and the pooled scores in summary are NA. The scores of the folds that finished, the failed assessment rows, the diagnostics, and the warnings all stay available, and errors names the stage and message of each failure. cv_tab() and select_cv() refuse an incomplete result rather than rank a model on its easier folds. A complete result says only that the calculations finished, so inspect diagnostics and warnings before you rank models.

What the scores do and do not include

The predictions and scores treat each fold's fitted parameters as known. They do not average over uncertainty in the coefficients or scales, give prediction intervals, or establish calibration. Compare candidates only on identical folds, assessment rows, responses, and weights, which cv_tab() checks for you. The scores complement aic_tab() but are not AIC values or Akaike weights. If you use the scores to choose a model, kernel, or metric, the winning score is optimistic. Assess the chosen procedure with an outer validation layer or an independent test set. select_cv() scores a predeclared training-AIC rule without this bias, because the assessment outcomes never choose the winner within a fold.

cross_validate() fits GLMs. For other model structures use cross_validate_mixed() (a random intercept for repeated surveys), cross_validate_clogit() (step selection), cross_validate_field() (a spatial random field), or cross_validate_bayes() (Bayesian models). GAMs and unmarked models have no cross-validation function. cross_validate_glm() scores reference models without scales on the same folds.

See also

multiScaleR_cv for the returned object, cross_validate_glm() for reference models, cv_tab() and select_cv() to compare candidates, grouped_cv_folds() and spatial_cv_folds() to build folds, and vignette("v08-cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR") for the full workflow.

Examples

data("landscape_counts")   # counts and one site-level covariate
data("surv_pts")           # 100 survey locations
pts <- vect(surv_pts)

# Folds are lists of row IDs, so build and check them before any fitting.
# The simulated coordinates are in meters, and crs = 32617 declares that.
folds <- spatial_cv_folds(crds(pts), block_size = 1000, k = 3, crs = 32617)
folds   # rows fitted (analysis) and held out (assessment) in each fold
#> Cross-validation folds: spatial 
#>   fold analysis assessment excluded
#>  fold1       66         34        0
#>  fold2       67         33        0
#>  fold3       67         33        0

# \donttest{
land <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif", package = "multiScaleR"))
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land[[c("land1", "land2")]],
                      max_D = 1000, kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
# Row names of dat match those of inputs$kernel_dat ("1" to "100")
dat <- data.frame(landscape_counts, inputs$kernel_dat)

# Scales and coefficients are estimated from the analysis rows of each fold
cv <- cross_validate(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, data = dat,
                     kernel_inputs = inputs, folds = folds,
                     family = "poisson", keep_selection = TRUE)
cv            # pooled held-out scores, lower is better
#> Cross-validation: 3 of 3 folds scored; 100 of 100 input rows assessed.
#>         metric estimate        unit n_assessment n_scored weight_sum complete
#>           rmse 1.648342 observation          100      100        100     TRUE
#>            mae 1.237010 observation          100      100        100     TRUE
#>  neg_log_score 1.628450 observation          100      100        100     TRUE
#>       deviance 1.290161 observation          100      100        100     TRUE
cv$complete   # TRUE: every fold was fitted and scored
#> [1] TRUE

# Sigma (map units) estimated in each fold. Similar values across folds
# suggest that no single block of surveys drives the estimated scales.
round(sapply(cv$training, function(fold) fold$scale_est$Mean))
#>      fold1 fold2 fold3
#> [1,]   236   246   239
#> [2,]   558   541   566

# Compare with a reference model that has no landscape covariates
site_cv <- cross_validate_glm(counts ~ site, dat, folds, family = "poisson",
                              keep_selection = TRUE)
cv_tab(list(landscape = cv, site_only = site_cv), metric = "rmse")
#>    Modnames Rank    Score     Delta Metric        Unit N_assessment N_scored
#> 1 landscape    1 1.648342 0.0000000   rmse observation          100      100
#> 2 site_only    2 2.232857 0.5845151   rmse observation          100      100
#>   Weight_sum Warnings
#> 1        100        0
#> 2        100        0
# }
